strengths: Clear and well-motivated two-stage framework that decouples behavior learning from planning principle alignment, with an appealing analogy to the LLM pretrain-then-RLHF paradigm; the motivating analysis (e.g., ~11.2% of nuPlan scenes exhibit speeding) is a nice empirical observation

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art reactive closed-loop scores on Val14 (84.97), Test14-hard (73.18), and Test14-random (94.51), outperforming strong baselines such as Diffusion Planner by +2.17 to +5.96 points; also competitive in the non-reactive setting, showing fine-tuning does not destroy expert-like behavior

Use of interpretable, rule-based rewards rather than costly preference data distinguishes the approach from TrajHF and Gen-Drive, and the multiplicative safety-indicator x weighted-cost reward structure (Eq. 4) is sensible for safety-critical planning

Reasonably thorough ablations: fine-tuning stage contribution (+6.08 score with per-metric breakdown), KL regularization weight sensitivity (Fig. 4), and pass@k analysis (Fig. 5) showing fine-tuning improves the likelihood of feasible samples, not just single-shot performance
Qualitative case study (Fig. 2) convincingly demonstrates that imitation-based planners replicate expert speeding while Plan-R1 corrects it, directly supporting the paper's central claim
Dual-model rollout design (frozen world model + trainable ego policy) is a pragmatic and clearly explained solution for stable multi-agent RL fine-tuning
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: tokenization (K-disk from Trajeglish), the factorized-attention architecture (from MotionLM/SMART/SceneTransformer), and the reward structure (following nuPlan/Gen-Drive metrics) are all adopted from prior work; the core contribution is essentially applying GRPO-style RL fine-tuning to an existing autoregressive planner, which is an incremental combination of known components

Potential reward-metric circularity is not addressed: the rule-based rewards (collision, drivable area, speed limit, comfort) are essentially the same components that constitute the CLS evaluation metrics, so the reported gains may partly reflect direct optimization of the test metric rather than genuinely safer planning; a discussion or an evaluation on metrics not used in the reward would strengthen the claim

Missing ablation on the reward components themselves (which of the safety/cost terms contribute how much), and no empirical comparison with PPO despite the motivation that GRPO is superior for this task

No discussion of the train/test simulation mismatch: fine-tuning rollouts use a learned frozen world model for surrounding agents, while evaluation uses replayed agents (NR) or IDM (R); the effect of this mismatch on the reported gains is unanalyzed

Reproducibility concerns in the main text: reward implementation details, hyperparameters (group size G, KL coefficient beta for the main runs, learning rates, model size), and compute cost are deferred to an appendix not included in the manuscript; minor typos ('finetning', 'Dual-Moel') suggest insufficient polish
Missing runtime/latency analysis for autoregressive closed-loop planning, which is important for the practical significance of the method
Ablations are conducted only on the reactive Test14-random setting; the KL-weight and pass@k analyses would be more convincing if replicated across splits or settings

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a logical progression from motivation to method to experiments.

The motivation is sensible: expert demonstrations contain unsafe behaviors (e.g., the reported 11.2% speeding statistic), and explicitly aligning a pretrained planner with rule-based rewards is a reasonable way to decouple behavior learning from safety compliance.
The dual-model rollout design (frozen world model for surrounding agents + trainable ego policy) is a sensible engineering choice for stable multi-agent RL fine-tuning.

Evaluation covers the standard nuPlan splits (Val14, Test14-random, Test14-hard) in both non-reactive and reactive settings, and includes ablations (KL weight, pass@k) that go beyond a single headline table.
The reactive closed-loop gains over prior learning-based planners (e.g., +2 to +6 points over Diffusion Planner) are non-trivial if they hold up.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is essentially combining well-known motion-token autoregressive modeling (MotionLM, Trajeglish, SMART) with GRPO (a direct transfer from DeepSeekMath) and rule-based rewards that largely mirror nuPlan's own metric components. Prior work such as Gen-Drive and TrajHF already performs RL fine-tuning of generative driving policies; the delta here is using hand-crafted rewards instead of learned reward models, which is an incremental distinction rather than a new framework.

Missing key baseline: the paper motivates GRPO by claims about PPO's instability and memory overhead, but never empirically compares against PPO (or any other RL algorithm) for fine-tuning. The central algorithmic choice is thus unsupported by evidence within this domain.

Reward-evaluation circularity: the rule-based rewards (collision avoidance, drivable area, speed limit, comfort) directly overlap with the nuPlan scoring criteria. Optimizing the test metric as training reward undermines the claim of improved 'safety and feasibility' — it is closer to metric optimization than genuine capability gain, and this concern is not acknowledged or controlled for.

Mixed and selectively reported results: Plan-R1 is below Diffusion Planner and PLUTO on several non-reactive metrics (e.g., Test14-hard NR 77.79 vs. 80.08 for PLUTO), yet the abstract and conclusion claim blanket 'state-of-the-art performance.' The SOTA claim holds mainly in the reactive setting, and the headline Test14-random result (94.51) additionally relies on a rule-based post-processing module borrowed from prior work.

The strongest evidence for the core motivation (that RL fine-tuning removes unsafe behaviors inherited from expert data) rests on qualitative case studies of one or a few cherry-picked scenarios (Figures 2 and 3), with no quantitative analysis of behavior-distribution shift or safety violations across the full dataset.

Reproducibility is weak in the main text: reward function details, weights, tokenization parameters, model size, training hyperparameters, and compute budget are deferred to an appendix, and there is no mention of code release, random seeds, or variance across runs. Several closed-loop RL results on nuPlan are known to be sensitive to setup details.

Technical sloppiness undermines confidence: a typo in Equation 3 ('agent i' where the index is n), 'Dual-Moel' in Figure 1, missing entries in Table 1 for Plan-R1* on Test14-hard, and unsubstantiated explanatory claims (e.g., attributing reactive gains to 'exploration capability' without any experiment isolating this).

The claimed link to LLM-style alignment is largely rhetorical: the fine-tuning stage is standard RL with a KL penalty to a reference policy, and the 'planning principles P' conditioning in the formulation is never actually implemented as conditioning input in a meaningful sense — rewards are applied post-hoc at training time.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-motivated: the observation that ~11.2% of nuPlan expert scenes exhibit speeding provides concrete evidence for the claimed problem of inheriting unsafe behaviors from expert data.

The two-stage framework (autoregressive pretraining + GRPO fine-tuning with rule-based rewards) is sensibly designed, and the dual-model rollout with a frozen reactive world model is a reasonable mechanism for multi-agent RL fine-tuning.

Strong empirical gains in the reactive closed-loop setting (+2.17, +3.96, +5.96 over Diffusion Planner on Val14, Test14-hard, Test14-random), which is the more challenging and practically relevant evaluation mode.
The paper includes several useful ablations: fine-tuning stage (Table 2 with per-metric breakdown), KL regularization weight (Figure 4), and pass@k analysis (Figure 5).
Qualitative analyses (Figures 2 and 3) directly illustrate the central claim that RL fine-tuning removes unsafe behaviors inherited from expert demonstrations.
Positioning against concurrent preference-based approaches (TrajHF, Gen-Drive) is clear and the use of interpretable rule-based rewards is a defensible design choice.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper combines well-known existing components — motion-token autoregressive modeling (Trajeglish, MotionLM, SMART), GRPO (DeepSeekMath), and PDM-style rule-based rewards — without significant methodological innovation. RL fine-tuning of generative driving policies has also been explored (Gen-Drive, Carplanner), so the delta over prior work is mostly the reward source (rules vs. learned reward model), which is incremental.

The SOTA claim is overclaimed. Even with post-processing, Plan-R1* loses to Diffusion Planner* on Test14-hard (77.79 vs 78.87 NR; 80.97 vs 82.00 R), and without post-processing it trails Diffusion Planner on Test14-hard NR (75.31 vs 75.99) and several non-reactive metrics. SOTA holds mainly in the reactive setting on Val14 and Test14-random, but the abstract and conclusion state it unconditionally.

No ablation on the RL algorithm choice: the paper argues GRPO is better suited than PPO, but never empirically compares against a PPO baseline. There is also no ablation isolating the contribution of individual reward components, which is important given the reward design is a core contribution (details are deferred to an appendix not included in the main paper).

Reproducibility concerns: missing key details such as model size, group size G, RL training hyperparameters, reward weights, tokenization vocabulary size, compute budget, and no mention of code release. The reported improvement margins (e.g., +0.5 on some non-reactive metrics) are within what run-to-run variance could produce, yet no error bars or statistical significance tests are reported.

A potential train/eval mismatch is not discussed: fine-tuning rollouts use the frozen pretrained model as the reactive world model, while evaluation uses IDM agents. Whether the gains transfer under this mismatch deserves analysis.
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (nuPlan); no results on other datasets or any real-world/non-simulated evidence, which weakens the broader significance of the safety claims.

Minor presentation issues: typos in Table 2 ('finetning'), inconsistent naming (PlanR1 vs. Plan-R1), and the comfort metric slightly degrades (-0.16), which deserves more discussion than a passing remark.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: the two-stage paradigm (autoregressive pre-training on expert data + rule-based RL fine-tuning) is cleanly formulated, and the paper convincingly argues why principle alignment should be decoupled from behavior learning.

VD-GRPO is a simple, practical modification with a plausible analysis: the paper provides concrete evidence (Figure 4 advantage distributions, Figure 5 unsafe-group ratio, Table 2) that GRPO's per-group normalization dilutes rare safety-critical signals, and that removing variance normalization fixes it (+3.45 collision, +1.69 R-CLS over GRPO).

Strong empirical results on nuPlan: state-of-the-art reactive scores (87.69 Val14, 77.20 Test14-hard, 90.04 Test14-random), large margins over Diffusion Planner in reactive mode, and comparisons against a broad set of rule-based and learning-based baselines under both NR and R settings.

Comprehensive ablation studies: RL fine-tuning vs. pre-training only, VD-GRPO vs. GRPO, dual-model vs. GT replay vs. 2x-capacity baseline, group size, KL weight beta, scaling constant c, pass@k, and per-component reward ablations (Table 5). This level of experimental rigor is above average.

Useful dual-model design (trainable ego planner + frozen reactive world model) is well ablated: GT replay (87.44) vs. reactive WM (90.04) vs. capacity control (84.94), which supports that the gain is not merely from model size.

Honest positioning in related work: the paper explicitly acknowledges Dr.GRPO and articulates how its problem (multi-objective, safety-critical rewards in planning) differs from difficulty bias in LLM training.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is modest. VD-GRPO essentially removes the standard-deviation normalization (as in Dr.GRPO) and applies a fixed scaling constant; the delta from prior work is primarily a new domain observation rather than a new method. The claim of 'identifying a key limitation of GRPO' is more of an empirical finding for this reward structure than a general contribution.

Theoretical support for VD-GRPO is thin. The paper argues safety-violation groups should dominate gradients, but no analysis of long-run behavior is given: as unsafe groups become extremely rare (and eventually vanish from samples), their gradient contribution still disappears; fixed scaling changes when this happens but does not fundamentally resolve it. A formal or at least more careful analysis is missing.

Evaluation realism concerns: reactivity is modeled only via IDM, which is a simple, largely longitudinal car-following model; this limits the strength of claims about 'realistic reactive settings' and multi-agent interaction awareness. No evaluation on other simulators (e.g., CARLA) or safety-critical scenario suites to test generalization of the safety claims.

Non-reactive results do not clearly surpass Diffusion Planner (94.72/94.64 vs. 94.26/94.80, and 78.46 vs. 78.87 on Test14-hard), and the headline Val14 numbers rely on applying an external post-processing/refinement module (Sun et al., 2024); the 'state-of-the-art' claim is thus qualified and partly inherited from other components.

Potential failure modes of the approach are not examined: reward hacking or overly conservative behaviors from the multiplicative zeroing of rewards (partially visible in the progress drop from 94.11 to 91.94 with VD-GRPO), and error accumulation/exploitation of the frozen world model during long rollouts are not discussed.

Generalization is untested: a single small model (5M params) on a single benchmark; it is unclear whether the two-stage recipe and VD-GRPO benefits transfer to other datasets, planning horizons, or end-to-end settings.

Minor presentation issues: cross-references in text appear broken ('In subsection 3.1, subsection 3.2...'), Figure 3 is cited where Table 3 is meant in the dual-model ablation discussion, and Table 4 is referenced as 'Figure 4' in the group-size ablation, which hurts clarity.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation on nuPlan across three standard splits (Val14, Test14-hard, Test14-random) under both non-reactive and reactive settings, with comparisons against a wide range of rule-based and learning-based baselines
Substantial ablation coverage: rule-based RL fine-tuning, VD-GRPO vs. GRPO, dual-model rollout vs. GT replay, group size, KL weight, scaling constant, reward components, pass@k, and model capacity

Clear and well-written presentation; the motivation that expert demonstrations contain undesirable behaviors (e.g., >10% speeding in nuPlan) is concrete and the qualitative trajectory visualizations effectively illustrate the point
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Figures 8-9) and implementation details (Appendix D) support reasonable reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: VD-GRPO (centering + fixed scaling, removing per-group standard deviation) is essentially Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), which the authors themselves cite; the only difference is a fixed constant c and its application to planning. The central algorithmic contribution is therefore a minor re-instantiation of existing work, and no theoretical or systematic analysis is provided for why fixed scaling is preferable in this domain

The overall framework (autoregressive trajectory tokenization + pre-training + rule-based RL fine-tuning) is an assembly of well-established components (MotionLM/Trajeglish-style tokenization, GRPO, Gen-Drive/TrajHF-style two-stage fine-tuning). The claimed 'new perspective' of planning as principle-aligned prediction is not genuinely new

Potential circularity in the reactive evaluation: the R-CLS metric uses IDM-based reactive agents, and the fine-tuning rewards are rule-based formulations aligned with the same nuPlan metric family (collision, drivable area, speed limit). The large reactive-setting gains (+5 to +8 points) may partly reflect optimizing against rule-based dynamics that mirror the evaluation's rule-based simulator, and this confound is not analyzed

No statistical reliability: results appear to be single runs with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, despite differences between methods in Table 1 sometimes being small (e.g., 88.98 vs. 89.87 NR-CLS on Val14)
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (nuPlan); no generalization evidence on other planning benchmarks (e.g., WOMD, CARLA) or in a world-model/planning context beyond the IDM simulator

The fine-tuning set is reduced to 100K scenarios for computational reasons, and the relationship between the fine-tuning distribution and the evaluation splits is not discussed; the 'state-of-the-art' claim also relies on mixing rows with rule-based post-processing (*) versus without in Table 1, complicating fair comparison

Internal inconsistencies suggest haste: the group-size ablation text references 'Figure 4' while the results are in Table 4; the reward 'w/o Collision' ablation reportedly drops NR-CLS to 73.10 while the Collision metric itself (94.15) barely changes relative to the full model (97.32), which is not explained; Table 2 ablation scores and Table 1 main results use different values without clear protocol clarification

The key empirical claim underlying VD-GRPO (Figure 4, safe/unsafe advantage distributions) is only supported qualitatively; no quantitative decomposition of gradient contributions from safe vs. unsafe groups is provided
Small model scale (~5M parameters) is fine for efficiency, but scaling behavior is only probed with a single 2x capacity ablation, leaving the generality of the conclusions unclear

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: decoupling behavior learning (imitation pre-training) from principle alignment (rule-based RL) is a sensible adaptation of the LLM training paradigm to trajectory planning, and the paper articulates the motivation (expert data lacking safety-critical coverage, inheriting undesirable behaviors) convincingly.

The analysis of GRPO's limitation in multi-objective planning is the most interesting contribution: the observation that per-group variance normalization erases cross-group reward scale differences, diluting rare safety-critical signals, is well explained and empirically supported by the advantage distribution analysis (Figure 4) and the unsafe-group ratio curves (Figure 5).

Strong empirical results on nuPlan, especially in the reactive setting (+4.89 to +7.98 over Diffusion Planner on R-CLS), which is the more realistic and challenging evaluation mode; the paper is honest that NR results only 'match' rather than clearly beat Diffusion Planner.

Comprehensive ablations: rule-based RL vs. VD-GRPO, dual-model/world-model design vs. GT replay vs. capacity increase, reward component removal, group size, KL weight, and scaling constant; the pass@k analysis in the appendix is a nice addition.

The dual-model design (trainable ego planner + frozen reactive world model) is a practical solution to non-stationarity during RL fine-tuning, and the ablation against a 2x-capacity baseline credibly attributes gains to the design rather than model size.
Good reproducibility: implementation details (architecture, ~5M params, hyperparameters, 8x RTX 4090) are provided, and reward design is documented in detail.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty of VD-GRPO: replacing per-group standard-deviation normalization with centering plus a fixed constant is very close to Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), which the authors acknowledge. The delta is the application and the domain-specific analysis rather than a fundamentally new method; the scaling constant c is essentially a learning-rate-like hyperparameter whose sensitivity is shown in Figure 9.

The theoretical justification for VD-GRPO is thin. Removing normalization makes gradient magnitudes depend on absolute reward scales, which could destabilize training or amplify large deviations from non-safety terms as well; the paper argues dominance of safety signals empirically but does not formalize when centering-only advantages prioritize safety versus merely amplifying whatever has the largest reward deviation.

Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (nuPlan). No experiments on Waymo, CARLA, or other simulators/datasets, which weakens claims of generality; the model is also small (5M params), so scaling behavior is unexplored.

SOTA claims need qualification: in the non-reactive setting and on Test14-hard NR, Plan-R1 does not surpass Diffusion Planner (78.46 vs. 78.87), and several rule-based/hybrid baselines use post-processing; the strongest gains are confined to the reactive IDM setting, where the comparison regime differs from how the method trains (learned world model) versus how baselines are simulated.

The reactive world model is simply a frozen copy of the pre-trained predictor; its reaction realism is not validated (e.g., no comparison of world-model rollouts against logged counterfactual agent behavior), so the claimed 'realistic multi-agent interactions' during fine-tuning is asserted rather than measured.

Some presentation issues: cross-references are occasionally wrong (group-size ablation refers to 'Figure 4' but reports Table 4), the safety-critical group variance argument is stated twice at length with heavy repetition, and the GRPO/VD-GRPO motivation would benefit from a small worked example clarifying how normalization flips relative advantage magnitudes.

Reward weighting (TTC w=5, comfort w=2, etc.) and the trajectory-level reward broadcasting to tokens are heuristic choices with limited justification; the reward-component ablation is single-seed and small deltas (e.g., +0.39 drivable area) are not accompanied by variance estimates or statistical significance tests.
